result: TOPBP1 and its homologues (Rad4 in fission yeast) are multi-BRCT domain scaffold proteins that mediate phosphorylation-dependent protein interactions in DNA replication, repair, and damage signaling. Vertebrate TOPBP1 contains nine BRCT domains, of which four N-terminal domains (BRCT1,2 and 4,5) are conserved in yeasts. Only a subset of these BRCT domains (three in yeast, four in vertebrates) possess the residues required to bind phosphorylated peptide motifs, and these domains display selectivity and specificity for their phosphopeptide ligands.
evaluation: Claims C1-C14 establish the structural and functional context for TOPBP1/Rad4 proteins based on established knowledge and prior literature (C7-C14 cite Garcia et al., 2005; Wardlaw et al., 2014; Leung et al., 2011-2013; Rappas et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2017). These background claims are well-supported by citations and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

result: The crystal structure of chicken TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2 in complex with phosphorylated RAD9-pS387 peptide was determined at 2.3 Å resolution. The structure reveals that RAD9-pS387 binds specifically to BRCT1 (not BRCT0 or BRCT2) with the peptide running perpendicular to the BRCT domain array. The phosphate group of pS387 is recognized by conserved residues Thr114, Arg121, and Lys155, while the peptide adopts a tight turn conformation that projects hydrophobic residues Leu383 (−4) and Ala384 (−3) into an extended hydrophobic pocket on BRCT1.
evaluation: Claims C22-C34 describe the crystal structure determination and detailed molecular interactions observed in the TOPBP1-RAD9 complex. The structural data (C22, deposited as PDB 6HM5) and detailed interaction descriptions (C23-C34) are supported by crystallographic evidence shown in Figure 1. Prior work (C15-C21) establishing RAD9-pS387 as a TOPBP1-binding site is well-cited (Lee et al., 2007; Rappas et al., 2011; Takeishi et al., 2010).

result: Systematic mutagenesis of the RAD9 peptide using pull-down assays revealed position-specific requirements for TOPBP1-BRCT1 binding. Position −3 (Ala) tolerates only valine substitution; position −4 (Leu) tolerates Phe or Ile with reduced binding; position −5 (Val) shows greatest tolerance including proline and polar residues (except Asp); position −1 (Asp) tolerates serine but not leucine or lysine substitutions.
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 describe peptide pull-down experiments shown in Figure 1D that systematically test amino acid substitutions at key positions. The data support the structural model by demonstrating which residues are critical for binding. The interpretation that position −5 is primarily involved in intrapeptide interactions (C38) is a reasonable inference from the structural data, though the explanation for Asp unfavorability (C39) is speculative.

result: Crystal structures of Rad4-BRCT1,2 bound to Sld3 bis-phosphorylated peptide (pT636-pT650) and comparison with previously determined Rad4-Crb2 complexes reveal that peptides binding to BRCT1 share a common tight turn conformation in the −5, −4, −3 region with conserved hydrophobic triplets. In contrast, peptides binding to BRCT2 maintain an extended β-sheet conformation upstream of the phosphorylated residue without the tight turn.
evaluation: Claims C43-C47 describe new crystal structure data (Rad4-Sld3 complex, deposited as PDB 6HM3, shown in Figure 2A) and structural comparisons with prior work (C42, Qu et al., 2013). The structural alignments shown in Figures 2B and 2C support the conclusions about distinct conformations for BRCT1 versus BRCT2-binding peptides. The inference about sequence conservation reflecting structural propensity (C45) is reasonable based on the data.

result: Structural analysis reveals the molecular basis for BRCT1 versus BRCT2 selectivity. Both domains have a hydrophobic recess that accommodates a hydrophobic residue at position −3, but BRCT1 has an extended recess that can accommodate two consecutive hydrophobic residues (−3 and −4) when the peptide adopts a tight turn. BRCT2's recess is restricted by a conserved tryptophan (Trp158 in Rad4, Trp257 in human TOPBP1), accommodating only a single hydrophobic residue and requiring extended β-sheet conformation. Sequences with large polar residues at −4 are restricted to BRCT2 binding.
evaluation: Claims C48-C56 present a structural model explaining BRCT domain specificity based on crystal structures shown in Figure 3. The model is well-supported by structural data (C49-C53) and binding experiments. The inferences about binding requirements (C54-C56) are logical extensions of the structural observations, though they represent interpretations rather than direct measurements.

result: Binding specificity studies with Treslin and other peptides demonstrate that BRCT2 is less selective than BRCT1 beyond requiring a hydrophobic −3 residue. Treslin-pT969 (with small polar Ser at −4) binds preferentially to BRCT2 as a short peptide, though this preference is diminished in longer peptides. Some sequences (Crb2-pT187, Treslin-pS1001) can bind both BRCT1 and BRCT2 with comparable affinity, but ability to bind BRCT1 does not guarantee BRCT2 binding (e.g., RAD9-pS387 binds BRCT1 with low micromolar affinity but weakly to BRCT2).
evaluation: Claims C57-C63 describe fluorescence polarization binding data shown in Figure 3E and referenced binding studies. The data support differential selectivity between BRCT1 and BRCT2. The observation about context-dependence (C58) is supported by citation to Boos et al., 2011. The inferences about selectivity (C59, C62) are reasonable generalizations from the binding data presented.

result: Many TOPBP1/Rad4-binding sites have a proline at position +1 following the phosphorylated Ser/Thr and are targets for CDKs or proline-directed kinases. Structural analysis shows the +1 residue is directed away from the BRCT domain and makes no direct contribution to binding specificity in either BRCT1 or BRCT2.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 describe a pattern observed in binding sites (supported by citations to Boos et al., 2011; Qu et al., 2013) and structural interpretation. The inference that +1 residue doesn't contribute to specificity (C66) is reasonable based on crystal structures showing this position directed away from the protein, though this is an interpretation rather than direct experimental test.

result: A novel TOPBP1-binding site was identified in human RHNO1 at Thr202 using bioinformatic analysis based on the defined BRCT-binding motifs. The RHNO1-pT202 peptide binds TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2 with sub-micromolar affinity specifically through BRCT1 (not BRCT2, BRCT4,5, or BRCT7,8), in a phosphorylation-dependent manner. The motif has characteristics of a proline-directed kinase site with a hydrophobic triplet at −5, −4, −3 positions and is highly conserved across metazoan RHNO1 homologues.
evaluation: Claims C71-C78 describe identification and characterization of a new TOPBP1-binding site using the specificity rules derived from structural studies. The bioinformatic prediction (C71, shown in Figure 4A) is validated by fluorescence polarization binding data (C75-C78, Figure 4B-D) and mutagenesis with BRCT1/BRCT2-specific mutations. Conservation analysis (C74, Figure 4 supplement 1) supports biological relevance. The characterization as a proline-directed kinase site (C72-C73) is inference based on sequence features.

result: Truncation mutations in RHNO1 that eliminate the region containing the Thr202 phosphorylation site have been identified in families with hereditary pancreatic cancer.
evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2016. This provides potential clinical relevance for the identified RHNO1-TOPBP1 interaction, though the functional significance requires further investigation.

result: Mdb1, the S. pombe orthologue of MDC1, contains a single SDT motif (unlike the six SDT repeats in mammalian MDC1). The Mdb1 bis-phosphorylated SDT peptide (pS216, pT218) binds S. pombe Nbs1 with sub-micromolar affinity but shows no binding to Rad4-BRCT1,2 or BRCT3,4, contrasting with the reported low-affinity interaction of mammalian MDC1 SDT repeats with TOPBP1-BRCT4,5.
evaluation: Claims C80-C87 establish the context for Mdb1 (C80-C85 supported by citations to Wei et al., 2014; Chapman and Jackson, 2008; Melander et al., 2008; Leung et al., 2013) and present new binding data (C86-C87, Figure 5A) showing the SDT motif does not mediate Rad4 interaction in fission yeast, motivating the search for alternative binding sites.

result: A novel Rad4-binding site was identified in Mdb1 at Thr113 using bioinformatic analysis. The Mdb1-pT113 peptide binds Rad4-BRCT1,2 with low micromolar affinity specifically through BRCT2 (not BRCT1), as predicted by the structural model due to the polar threonine at position −4. Crystal structure of Rad4-BRCT1,2 with Mdb1-pT113 peptide confirms BRCT2 binding with the valine at −3 in the hydrophobic pocket and the polar Thr at −4 directed to solvent in an extended β-sheet conformation.
evaluation: Claims C88-C98 describe identification of a new Rad4-binding site through bioinformatic prediction (C88-C89, supported by citations to Beltrao et al., 2012; Ullah et al., 2016), prediction of BRCT2 specificity based on the structural model (C90-C91), experimental validation by mutagenesis (C94, Figure 5C), and crystal structure determination (C95-C98, PDB 6HM4, Figure 5D-E). The data strongly support the predictive power of the BRCT specificity model.

result: The biological significance of the Mdb1-pT113 site requires further investigation, as Mdb1 deletion shows DNA damage phenotypes only in specific genetic backgrounds. However, analogous TOPBP1-binding sites in mammalian MDC1 appear to function in mitotic DNA damage response.
evaluation: Claim C99 acknowledges that functional validation is incomplete, appropriately noting this as future work. Claim C100 references an unpublished manuscript (Ahorner, Jones et al., manuscript submitted), which cannot be fully evaluated. The biological relevance of the identified site remains to be established.

result: TOPBP1 and its homologues interact with multiple ligand proteins in phosphorylation-dependent manner, including DNA topoisomerase II, Treslin/Sld3, 53BP1/Crb2, MDC1, the 9-1-1 clamp, and helicases BLM and FANCJ. This study adds RHNO1 and Mdb1 to this group, with additional phosphorylation-dependent ligands likely yet to be identified.
evaluation: Claims C101-C107 summarize known TOPBP1 interactions supported by multiple citations (Broderick et al., 2015; Yamane et al., 1997; Boos et al., 2011; Kumagai et al., 2010; Cescutti et al., 2010; Qu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Delacroix et al., 2007; Furuya et al., 2004; Blackford et al., 2015; Gong et al., 2010) and the new data from this study. Claim C108 is reasonable speculation based on the findings.

result: The N-terminal BRCT module (BRCT1 and BRCT2) displays clear and distinctive specificities for ligand binding, with similar specificities likely for the central BRCT module (BRCT4,5) and C-terminal module (BRCT7,8). Limited high-affinity interactions have been characterized for the central module (S. pombe Rad9 peptide to BRCT4, BLM peptide to BRCT5) and C-terminal module (FANCJ peptide to BRCT7,8).
evaluation: Claim C110 is directly supported by the experimental data presented. Claim C111 is reasonable inference by analogy. Claims C112-C116 summarize known interactions from cited literature (Qu et al., 2013; Blackford et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2017; Leung et al., 2011), noting limited characterization of these modules compared to BRCT1,2.

result: Based on BRCT domain specificities, some ligand combinations could potentially bind simultaneously to a single TOPBP1/Rad4 molecule (e.g., 9-1-1 via BRCT1 and BLM via BRCT5), while other combinations are mutually exclusive due to competition for the same binding site (e.g., RHNO1 and RAD9 both bind BRCT1; Treslin and 9-1-1 compete in metazoa). Competition may be resolved by differential binding affinities (RHNO1-pT202 binds ~10-fold tighter than RAD9-pS387) and cell cycle-regulated phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C117-C121 present logical inferences about possible and impossible ligand combinations based on the specificity data. Claim C120 explicitly contradicts a prior model (Lindsey-Boltz et al., 2015). Claim C122 is supported by binding affinity measurements. Claim C123 is reasonable speculation about regulatory mechanisms, though direct evidence for cell cycle regulation is limited (C124-C125 cite Pinna, 2002 for CK2 but RHNO1-pT202 as CDK target is inference).

result: Regulation of TOPBP1/Rad4 complex formation may involve differential kinase activities: RAD9-pS387 is generated by constitutively active CK2, while RHNO1-pT202 has characteristics of a CDK target potentially restricted to specific cell cycle phases. TOPBP1 may also oligomerize via AKT-dependent phosphorylation under some circumstances, further complicating the regulatory landscape.
evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by citation (Pinna, 2002), but C125 is speculative inference based on sequence features without experimental validation of CDK phosphorylation or cell cycle regulation. Claim C126 is supported by citation (Liu et al., 2006) but represents an additional complexity not directly investigated in this study.

result: The findings suggest that TOPBP1-BRCT domain interactions could be targeted therapeutically for cancer treatment. While previous efforts have been limited by poor cell permeability of inhibitors targeting phosphate interactions, the demonstration that specificity and high-affinity binding is mediated by predominantly hydrophobic interactions suggests these should be more amenable to competitive blockade by cell-penetrant small molecules.
evaluation: Claims C127 and C129 are speculative statements about potential therapeutic applications. While the structural findings (that hydrophobic interactions drive specificity) are well-supported, the claim that this makes drug development more tractable (C129) is speculation without experimental validation. Claim C128 about limitations of prior approaches is supported by citation (Yuan et al., 2011).
